evidence.paraphrase: The narrator sets the tale in a specific past year and remote African locale.
evidence.quote:
It was, I think, in the March of '69 that I was up in Sikukuni's
country.

evidence.paraphrase: Quatermain is deeply affected by his son's death and abandons England.
evidence.quote:
the death of his only son so unsettled him that he immediately
left England

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator explains the mist as fever vapor rising from rotting vegetation.
evidence.quote:
It was the fever mist. Out from among the
scrub, too, came little spirals of vapour, as though there were hundreds
of tiny fires alight in it--reek rising from thousands of tons of
rotting vegetation.

evidence.paraphrase: An entire village has been wiped out by fever, leaving only one old woman.
evidence.quote:
she told me that all the people whom I had seen had died of fever. When
they had died the other inhabitants of the kraal had taken the cattle
and gone away, leaving the poor old woman

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator contrasts native practice with a scientific-sounding principle for the reader.
evidence.quote:
Those people carry the doctrine of the survival of
the fittest to its extreme, you see.

evidence.paraphrase: Quatermain gives a practical explanation of a lion's vulnerability compared to a buck.
evidence.quote:
The lion is soft, and not a difficult animal
to finish if you hit him anywhere in the body. A buck takes far more
killing.

evidence.paraphrase: The hunter systematically investigates where the lions rest during the day.
evidence.quote:
the first thing I set to work to do was to try to
discover whereabouts the brutes lay up for the day

evidence.paraphrase: He reasons from wind direction to devise a plan to burn out the lions.
evidence.quote:
there was a
strong wind blowing from the direction of the waggon, across the reedy
pan towards the bush-clad kloof or donga, and this first gave me the
idea of firing the reeds

evidence.paraphrase: The narrator describes his terror while lions feed near him.
evidence.quote:
there I lay shaking
with terror, and the cold perspiration pouring out of me

evidence.paraphrase: A burst cartridge case fouls the breech so a new round won't seat, explaining the gun's failure.
evidence.quote:
when I tried to get in the new
cartridge it would only enter half-way

evidence.paraphrase: The lasting injury permanently marks the narrator's body.
evidence.quote:
I have been lame ever
since, and shall be to my dying day; in the month of March the wound
always troubles me a great deal, and every three years it breaks out
raw.

evidence.paraphrase: The framing describes a quest into an unexplored interior for a rumored hidden white people.
evidence.quote:
He is persuaded that a white people, of which he
has heard rumours all his life, exists somewhere on the highlands in the
vast, still unexplored interior
